## Atomic scale etching of diamond: insights from molecular dynamics simulations

Jack S Draney1, Joseph R Vella2, Athanassios Z Panagiotopoulos1 and David B Graves1,∗

1 Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08540, United States of America 2 Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Princeton, NJ 08540, United States of America

E-mail: dgraves@princeton.edu

Received 19 March 2024, revised 31 July 2024 Accepted for publication 10 September 2024 Published 16 October 2024

Abstract Diamond is a promising material for multiple applications in quantum information processing and sensing as well as applications in microelectronics. However, diamond devices can be limited by surface defects that compromise charge stability and spin coherence, among others. Improved strategies in plasma etching of diamond could play an important role in minimizing or eliminating these defects. In this work, we explore plasma-assisted atomic scale etching of diamond using argon ions (Ar+), hydrogen ions (H+) and hydrogen atoms (H). We employ classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and test several interatomic potentials based on the Reactive Empirical Bond Order (REBO) form with comparisons to a variety of published experimental results. We performed MD simulations of low-energy hydrogen (⩽50 eV) and argon (⩽200 eV) ion bombardment of diamond surfaces. Ar+ bombardment can be used to locally smooth initially rough diamond surfaces via the formation of an amorphous C layer, the thickness of which increases with argon ion energy. Subsequent exposure with hydrogen ions (or fast neutrals) will selectively etch this amorphous C layer, leaving the underlying diamond layer mostly intact if the H energy is maintained below about 10 eV. The simulations suggest that combining Ar+ smoothing with selective, near threshold energy H removal of amorphous C can be an effective strategy for diamond surface engineering, leading to more reliable and sensitive diamond color center devices.

Supplementary material for this article is available online

Keywords: diamond, molecular dynamics, hydrogen, etching

## 1. Introduction

Current and future advanced applications of diamond, such as high-power electronics and nanoscale quantum sensing, can

be compromised by surface defects [1–3]. Plasma in various forms and under various conditions is used extensively in diamond processing, from epitaxial growth to doping to etching and various surface modifications. For example, controlling plasma etch damage for near-surface nitrogen vacancy (NV) color centers in quantum grade diamond is essential for minimizing loss of quantum coherence and the generation of associated magnetic noise [3, 4]. Following growth and doping of diamond (typically via microwave plasma chemical vapor deposition), the material generally must be processed further to prepare the surface and

make functional devices. Controlling diamond surface chemistry is difficult because of its relative chemical inertness and due to challenges in preparing flat diamond surfaces with uniform properties. Diamond surfaces are typically mechanically polished after growth to obtain smooth surfaces, but the resulting surface is highly strained to depths of several microns [3]. Subsequent conventional plasma etching (sometimes referred to as reactive ion etching or RIE) will remove this strained layer, but plasma etching can be difficult to control and can result in major variability in surface morphology and surface termination. This is an especially serious problem in the case of diamond surfaces to be used for quantum sensing because of the extreme sensitivity of the resulting devices to even a few nearby atomic scale defects [1–4]. The current best practices in color center device processing after RIE involve the use of a combination of vacuum annealing over many hours, followed by hot acid cleaning [3]. More annealing and acid cleaning steps may be used following subsequent ion implantation for dopant incorporation. However, even utilizing the current best practices in surface engineering, coherence times of shallow NV centers remain far from typical bulk values. There is a clear need to better understand plasma-diamond surface interactions in order to exploit the many potential strengths of plasma processing for this promising class of materials. The present article reports results from classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of argon ion (Ar+), hydrogen atoms (H) and hydrogen ions (H+) impacting diamond carbon (C) surfaces. The first set of studies reported here aim to assess the ability of the MD simulation protocol and the associated interatomic potentials to match the available experimental data. We examine published measurements of Ar+ impacting a diamond surface, creating an amorphous layer and physically sputtering C. Additional comparisons are made between measurements and MD simulations for etching hard hydrocarbon films with a combination of Ar+ and atomic H. Finally, we compare the available experimental data and MD simulation results for energetic H+ ions impacting graphitic carbon. As with virtually all plasma–surface interactions, impacts by Ar+ or H+ ions can significantly alter the near-surface properties in a variety of ways. In our study, we highlight the effects of Ar+ bombardment on diamond, creating an amorphous C region near the surface and how this can be utilized for local surface smoothing. H+ impacts from hyperthermal to 10 eV are shown to etch this amorphous carbon more rapidly than the underlying diamond, suggesting a possible processing protocol that can result in near-perfect diamond surfaces. We illustrate one version of this idea by showing how a sequential Ar+ amorphization followed by H+ hydrogenation and selective etching scheme can result in removal of most of the plasmagenerated near-surface damaged layer. This sequence is shown to leave only about one monolayer of damaged, hydrogenated carbon on the diamond surface. The present results illustrate how careful control of plasma processes and plasma–surface interactions will be needed to more fully exploit plasma for critical applications such as diamond color center device processing. The range of possible

conditions and plasma chemistries that can be utilized is large and the field is in need of systematic studies combining experiment and computation. Atomistic simulations of plasma–surface interactions such as those presented here will be most useful when combined with well-defined and controlled plasma, material and surface science experiments.

## 2. Methods

2.1. Setup

Simulations are performed with the LAMMPS [5] simulation package (version 29 December 2022) using the inbuilt ‘rebo’ style for the second-generation REBO potential [6] (REBO2) and the REBO2-S potential from Atomistica library v1.1.0 for the screened REBO potential developed by Pastweka et al [7] (REBO2-S). Many of the simulations were also repeated with the first generation REBO potential [8, 9] (REBO1) and AIREBO [10] in order to provide comparisons between a variety of REBO style potentials. Etch yields for these auxiliary potentials are reported in SI figure S1. Interactions with argon were modeled with the ZBL potential [11]. Ions are simulated as uncharged atoms, as it is assumed the ions are Auger neutralized before impact [12]. Treatment of H+ ions and H atoms differs only in terms of their initial velocities: incident H+ ions are given large velocities normal to the surface, while H atoms are introduced with velocities sampled from the Maxwell– Boltzmann distribution at the temperature of interest. Simulations performed on diamond substrates begin with a bare 2×1 reconstructed (001) surface. The boundary conditions are periodic in the x and y directions and ‘shrinkwrapped’ in the z direction, meaning the boundaries are fixed at some minimum distance but allowed to increase temporarily if atoms move beyond this distance, ensuring no atoms are lost. Simulation cells have varying surface areas, with the primary cell sizes being 6 unit cells by 6 unit cells in the x and y directions (hereafter referred to as the 6 × 6 cell) and 10 unit cells by 10 unit cells in the x and y directions (10 × 10). These correspond to areas of approximately 4.6 × 10−14 cm2 for the (6 × 6) cell and 1.27 × 10−13 cm2 for the (10 × 10) case. The total number of atoms in each simulation varies, but typically 6 × 6 cells contain 1000–3000 atoms, while 10 ×10 cells contain around 5000 atoms. Amorphous substrates are prepared by bombarding diamond surfaces with 200 eV Ar+ ions until steady state is reached. The lattice constant for each potential is set to the value that minimizes the potential energy of a diamond lattice at 0 K. Diamond’s low thermal expansion coefficient means the equilibrium lattice constant is negligibly higher around 300 K, where these simulations were performed, so this 0 K lattice constant is acceptable. The bottom two layers of the cell are fixed in place to prevent the cell from moving and to simulate a continuous diamond layer below.

2.2. Ion impact simulations

Ion impact simulations begin by placing an atom of the incident species at a random location above the surface, just

high enough that it is outside the interaction range of the potential, with a velocity normal to the surface corresponding to the ion energy of interest. The angular distribution of ions is not considered. The simulation is then integrated in the microcanonical ensemble (the energy, cell volume, and number of particles are conserved) using an adaptive timestep for 0.5 ps in the case of REBO2 and 1 ps in the case of REBO2- S. Increasing this time to 1 ps for REBO2 had no significant effect. An adaptive timestep is necessary, because the low mass and high velocity of incoming hydrogen ions leads to poor conservation of energy unless the timstep is on the order of 10−6 ps during the initial impact. An adaptive timestep allows the simulation to maintain this small timestep for the initial impact and then relax to a longer timestep once the ion has lost some of its kinetic energy. The adaptive timestep is set such that the fastest atom only moves 0.01 Å every step, but is restricted to a maximum value of 0.25 fs. Following the ion impact, any clusters which satisfy the following three conditions are removed and recorded: (i) they have detached from the surface by moving all their atoms outside the interaction range of the potential, (ii) they have a center of mass above the highest surface atom and (iii) they have a center of mass with a positive z velocity (directed away from the surface). If the incident ion is argon it is also removed at this point under the assumption that it would desorb during the inter-impact time in a real system. After this, a stratified Berendsen thermostat [13] as described by Vella and Graves [14] is applied for 0.5 ps with a constant timestep of 0.25 fs. The use of the Berendsen thermostat is justified in this case, as its purpose is to remove the excess energy deposited by the ion before the next ion impact, approximating the effect of the inter-impact cooling time. Because the reactions of interest are primarily ion-driven rather than thermally-driven, a perfect Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of energies is not necessary, and a Berendsen thermostat is sufficient. In simulations of simultaneous Ar+/H bombardment, the surface temperature is kept at 340 K to match the related experiments by Hopf et al [15]. In all other simulations, the surface temperature is kept at 300 K. After the application of the thermostat, detached clusters are again removed. At this point, if the number of carbon atoms is less than the initial number of carbon atoms in the simulation, layers of diamond are added to the bottom of the cell, two at a time, until the number of carbon atoms is again greater than the initial number of carbon atoms. This entire process is repeated, cumulatively, for thousands of impacts per simulation, well beyond the required fluence for the cell to reach steady state. The total simulated fluence for each simulation is listed in table S1 of the supplementary information.

2.3. Simultaneous bombardment of Ar+ and neutral H

We also simulate simultaneous exposure to both Ar+ and H atoms. If the starting substrate is diamond, the cell is first bombarded with only ions to reduce the time to steady state. If the starting substrate is amorphous, then this initial step is skipped. Next, hydrogen neutrals are introduced to the top of the simulation cell at 2100 K, with velocity components drawn from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, to match the conditions

of the experiment done by Hopf et al [15]. The z component of the velocity is restricted to be negative so the inserted atom will move toward the surface. The simulation is then allowed to evolve for 0.1 ps before the addition of another neutral atom. Introduction of neutrals is paused every 36 neutrals to apply a stratified thermostat for 0.5 ps. The simulation continues until a monolayer of neutrals has been introduced (a monolayer (ML) is defined as 1.6 × 1015 atoms cm−2, or 72 atoms for a 6 × 6 simulation cell.) After this, an ion impact is simulated as described in the previous paragraph, another thermostat is applied, and the entire process is repeated until the desired fluence of ions is reached. The total simulated fluence for each simulation is listed in table S1 of the supplementary information.

2.4. Analysis

Confidence intervals were primarily calculated by bootstrapping on block averages of a single trajectory. In other words, a single cumulative simulation was run for each case (e.g. for each energy, potential, etc). Once the simulation reached steady state, relevant values (e.g. hydrogen uptake, number of amorphous carbon) were recorded after every ML of fluence. Values were averaged in blocks to create independent samples, and these samples were fed into a bootstrapping algorithm to determine the confidence intervals. Not all confidence intervals were determined in this manner, though. For simulations which use an amorphous substrate, the amount of time the simulation can remain at steady state without reaching the diamond subsurface is limited, so block averages from the steady-state periods of three separate simulations are combined for bootstrapping. The exact block widths and fluences considered are outlined in table S1 of the supplementary information. Finally, confidence intervals for etch product distributions shown in figure 10 are based on the binomial distribution and are calculated using the etch products observed during the entire steady-state period. More precise details about how these error bars are calculated can be found in the supplementary information or the published plotting code [16]. We use three different metrics to describe the amorphous layer formed in these simulations: number of amorphous carbon atoms (measured in ML), amorphous layer thickness (measured in Å) and amorphous layer range (also measured in Å). To identify which atoms are in the diamond cubic phase, and by extension which are amorphous carbon, common neighbor analysis is performed on the second neighbors of each atom [17]. Every carbon atom identified to be diamond cubic by this technique, as well as its first and second neighbors, are counted as diamond, and all others are considered amorphous. This analysis is implemented as a LAMMPS compute using code from OVITO [18]. To determine amorphous layer thickness, we define the amorphous layer as the region where carbon density, as determined by summing Gaussian kernels with σ = a/8 centered at each atomic position, is between 10% and 90% that of diamond. This metric was designed to provide a measure of the amorphous layer that ignored the fluctuating ‘stringy’ structures that form above the surface, and which could be compared to

Surface roughness was determined by splitting the surface into unit cells, finding the height of the highest atom in each cell (or highest diamond atom, if finding the roughness of the underlying diamond subsurface), and taking the root-meansquare of their deviation from the average surface height. Values reported as a function of ion energies are averages of samples taken every 1 ML after the system had reached steady state and, for the amorphous substrates, before the etch front reached the underlying diamond. Error bars represent the 95% confidence interval, mainly as determined by bootstrapping block averages of these samples. For more details on error bars and block averaging, see the supplementary information.

## 3. Results and discussion

3.1. Comparison to Ar+ and Ar+/H beam experiments

For the first comparison between MD simulations and experiments, we use results of beam experiments from Hopf et al [15], Guzman de la Mata [19], Karahashi et al [20], and Cong et al [21]. In beam experiments, surfaces are exposed to known fluxes of species at controlled energies and the effects of these exposures are measured. Hopf et al used a ‘hard’ hydrocarbon film with a H/C ratio of 0.3, Karahashi et al used a carbon film containing essentially no hydrogen and a density of 1.85 g cm−3, Guzman de la Mata et al used a single crystal high pressure high temperature (HPHT) diamond substrate, and Cong et al used a polycrystalline diamond substrate grown in a PECVD reactor. For this set of comparisons we use the REBO2 C-H potentials in the MD simulations. Figure 1(a) plots predicted amorphous layer thickness for an initially crystalline diamond substrate as a function of Ar+ fluence for ion energies ranging from 50 eV to 200 eV. The amorphous layer thickness, as defined in the ‘Analysis’ section, is indicated by the dashed lines on the snapshot insets to figure 1(a). A steady state amorphous layer thickness is observed from the simulations after about 50 ML of Ar+ fluence for energies above about 100 eV. Figure 1(b) plots the approximate steady state amorphous layer thickness as a function of ion energy as well as the estimated thicknesses from the spectroscopic ellipsometry measurements of Cong et al [21]. The agreement between MD simulations and estimated measured thicknesses is good. We note that a similar Ar+

induced amorphization of initially crystalline Si was reported by Humbird et al [22], although the thickness of the amorphous diamond surfaces is smaller than that of Si for a given Ar+ energy. This is as expected since diamond is significantly harder than Si. A second important test of the MD simulations can be made by comparing steady state Ar+ sputtering yields and Ar+/H etch yields with experimental values. Figure 2 plots both of these quantities. The comparison between physical sputtering yields (average number of C atoms removed per incident Ar+) shows that the MD predictions are within the three sets of

experimental data from Hopf et al [15], Karahashi et al [20], and Guzman de la Mata et al [19]. It should be noted that the Hopf et al data were taken using a hydrogenated C film, the Karahashi et al data were taken using a nearly pure carbon film, and that both the MD simulations and the Guzman de la Mata et al data correspond to a diamond carbon substrate. But the Ar+ physical sputtering yields are similar for these materials under these conditions. The etch yield results from Hopf et al [15] from exposing the hydrogenated C substrate to a combined flux of Ar+ and H atoms, as expected, are about an order of magnitude higher than sputtering yield for Ar+ alone. Figure 2 shows two sets of etch yield results from MD simulations for this case. The squares correspond to predicted yield when the target is a preamorphized diamond substrate. This should correspond most closely to the experimental system in which a hydrogenated carbon film is the target. Calculated etch yields were scaled by 2.21 to adjust for differences in flux ratio between simulation and experiment (72 and 400, respectively) according to the flux ratio dependence reported by Hopf et al [15]. For comparison to subsequent calculations, shown below, involving H+-only impacts, figure 3 shows the layer side views after diamond is impacted with Ar+/H for energies ranging from 50 eV to 200 eV. In particular, the mixed near-surface regions with non-diamond carbon and H mixed together are relatively compact. Except for the point at 20 eV in figure 2, the agreement between the MD simulations using the pre-amorphized diamond target and the experiment is reasonably good. The relatively high measured yield value at 20 eV is difficult to explain and may require further investigation. In most ‘reactive ion etching’ observations for other materials (e.g. Si), we would expect 20 eV to be near or below the minimum ion energy threshold to induce etching (e.g. Vella et al [23]). It is possible that the relatively high apparent etch yield corresponding to 20 eV ions is due to a higher spontaneous etch yield for 0.2 eV H atoms than is accounted for in the simulations. But this interpretation would be inconsistent with the low etch yields associated with H+ ions at energies below about 5 eV as reported in the next section. The closed circles in figure 2 correspond to MD simulation results utilizing a diamond carbon substrate. At 100 eV and above, these results are nearly identical to the MD predictions using the pre-amorphized diamond layer (solid squares). It appears that the surface nanostructure affects etch yields significantly when ion energy approaches the threshold ion energy. We conclude from this section that the comparison between MD simulations using REBO2 potentials and experiment when surfaces are exposed to either Ar+ alone or to simultaneous fluxes of Ar+ and H atoms is generally good. The quality of the agreement is comparable to that observed in other systems (e.g. Si etching by Cl and Ar+ as reported by Vella et al [14, 23] and SiO2 etching [24]). As will be seen in the subsequent section, however, the agreement when energetic H+

is employed is less straightforward to interpret and appears to offer some unique challenges to the conventional use of MD simulations of plasma–surface interactions with REBO-style potentials.

3.2. Comparison of MD simulations to H+ beam experiments

To validate simulations where hydrogen is the sole energetic species etching or modifying the diamond surface, it would be ideal to compare simulations to experiments utilizing a well

characterized H+ ion beam system with a diamond substrate. Unfortunately, there appears to be few if any published experimental data for diamond substrate etch yields in the presence of characterized beams of H+ ions. There are, however, results for the effects of H+ ion beams on graphitic carbon surfaces, motivated primarily by interests in plasma-materials interactions in the plasma fusion community.

H+ ions with energies above a few eV will amorphize and hydrogenate the near-surface of the diamond substrate, suggesting that MD simulations of energetic H on diamond substrates will be similar to results for an amorphous target. But as we saw in the previous section, the identity of the underlying substrate can influence results when the energetic species impact at relatively low, near-threshold energies. Nevertheless, comparing MD results to these available experimental data was important in revealing some important apparent limitations to the use of REBO2 potentials for this application.

We have chosen to use the results of beam experiments from Mech et al [25] and Balden and Roth [26] to compare to MD simulations. Mech et al employed quadrupole mass spectrometer (QMS) estimates of etch products to obtain etch yields, and Balden and Roth employed direct substrate weight loss measurements. Both sets of investigators made similar, critical observations: (i) etch yield energy threshold for H+−C reactive ion etching is between 5–10 eV for normal incidence ions; and (ii) etch yield rises to a few percent and then remains approximately constant up to about 50 eV. This behavior of nearly constant yield with respect to impacting ion energy is qualitatively different from results observed in other systems in reactive ion etching or plasma etching. The etch yield vs. ion energy profiles illustrated in figure 2 are more typical. That is, above some threshold energy, yields rise approximately as the square root of ion energy.

Indeed, when using the REBO2 potential to simulate H ion etching of C at 300 K, etch yields rise monotonically from the 5–10 eV threshold to values well above those reported experimentally, as can be seen in figure 4(b). Other groups have also observed similar, significantly overestimated

Notably, non-cumulative simulations, which reset the surface after each impact, generally give etch yields which are much closer to those reported by experiments [27, 28, 30, 33, 34]. The fact that only cumulative simulations show these errors indicates that the development of the damaged layer is likely the source of the issue. It has been shown that MD simulations of amorphous carbon structures using these force fields fail to reproduce observed sp2 to sp3 carbon ratios, and, further, simulations using different force fields tend to disagree with each other on the overall morphology of amorphous layers [35–37]. By contrast, screened REBO potentials, which use screening functions to increase the interaction distance of REBO potentials and eliminate artifacts typically seen in the cutoff region, do a better job matching the hybridization ratios seen by DFT calculations and experiments [38, 39]. We therefore ran simulations using one version of the screened REBO potential developed by Pastewka et al that we refer to as REBO2-S [38].

We find when REBO2-S is employed in simulations of hydrogen ion bombardment, etch yields are much closer to the experimental results, even exhibiting the same plateau with respect to ion energy seen experimentally. This is illustrated

in figure 4(b). Despite this key difference, we observe that simulations using REBO2 and REBO2-S potentials give similar results for etch threshold, degree of surface damage, and hydrogen uptake. The latter two quantities are compared for the two potentials in figures 5(a) and (b), and they are clearly quite close to one another. Figure 5(a) plots number of amorphous carbon in the steady state amorphous layer created by hydrogen ion bombardment vs incoming hydrogen ion energy. Results using the two potentials are very similar using this metric. Figure 5(b) plots hydrogen uptake in the steady state amorphous layer vs incoming hydrogen ion energy. Results using the two potentials are very similar using this metric as well. Layers even exhibit similar atomic distributions in the surface layers. Plots of atomic density vs depth for each potential are included in figure S6 in the supplementary information.

The differences in the range of the amorphous layers and the corresponding differences in layer structure can be seen more clearly in the following two figures. Figure 8 plots the range of the amorphous layer vs ion fluence for 30 eV ions using both potentials. Circles indicate minimum and maximum ranges for both simulations. Side views of these cells at the highlighted minimum and maximum values of range are shown in figure 9. Horizontal lines on figure 9 show the positions of the lowest and highest amorphous carbon atoms. The left column in figure 9 shows results from a simulation performed with REBO2, and the right column shows from a simulation performed with REBO2-S. The REBO2 layers feature large, open, stringy structures above denser amorphous sub surfaces, while even the largest REBO2-S layer is still a coherent, interconnected bundle.

These large, stringy structures characteristic of layers using REBO2 mean more carbon is open and vulnerable to hydrogen impact. While the same surface area of carbon is subject to the initial hydrogen impact in both cases (since the hydrogen

enters normal to the amorphous surface), hydrogen’s small mass means relatively little energy is lost on its first collision, and deflected hydrogen remains significantly labile. In some cases, hydrogen can even become more reactive upon reflection. This is because more of its kinetic energy can be transferred, and thus far more chemistry can occur, in inelastic, bond-forming collisions, which only occur if the hydrogen ions are moving slowly enough to be captured by the dangling bond.

The stringy, open surfaces associated with REBO2 provide a larger surface area for these reflected hydrogen to attack. Stringiness will lead to strands or chunks of carbon that can be removed by breaking relatively few bonds. This will increase etch yields by removing more carbon per etching event. Figure 10 confirms that clusters larger than three carbon atoms contribute significantly to the observed yield from REBO2 simulations, while they are relatively unimportant in the REBO2-S simulations. The largest product seen in the 25 eV simulation performed with REBO2-S contained only 10 carbon atoms, while a simulation on the same cell size performed with REBO2 saw an etch product containing 91 carbon atoms. REBO2 etch yield distributions exhibit a long tail, showing how large etch products contribute significantly to the observed etch yields. By contrast, REBO2-S distributions show little to no contribution from products larger than 3 carbon atoms. Etch product distributions are discussed further in the supplementary information section.

The larger cutoff of REBO2-S implies that clusters must be farther from the nominal surface before being removed and counted as etch products in the simulation. It also means that simulations must increase the time per impact, since hydrogen must start farther from the surface. Both of these effects could create artifacts in the etching statistics. It has been verified that these changes do not in fact significantly affect the etch yield by repeating the 25 eV REBO2 simulation with the settings for the REBO2-S cluster cutoff and impact time. Etch yield was only slightly lower in this case, within statistical uncertainty.

3.3. Atomic scale etching of diamond

One potentially significant advantage of Ar+ ion beam treatment of diamond is surface smoothing. Ion beam smoothing has been extensively studied, including for diamond surfaces, and it appears to be possible to smooth initially rough diamond surfaces significantly using this approach [40–42]. Conventional low-pressure plasma reactive ion etching, which involves the simultaneous bombardment of surfaces with both energetic ions and reactive neutrals, tends to induce surface roughness. In contrast, atomic layer etching (ALE), which separates bombardment of energetic inert ions and reactive neutrals has been shown to significantly smooth rough surfaces

We turn to the use of energy-controlled H+ to achieve this desired result.

There is significant evidence that H radicals can selectively remove amorphous carbon from diamond (e.g. Butler et al [44]). However, this role of H has been most commonly explored under the relatively high pressure (tens to hundreds of torr) and high temperature (on the order of 1000 ◦C– 1500 ◦C), conditions that are used during plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition of diamond. Typically, growth is conducted with mostly H2 and a small amount of CH4. It has been postulated that the H2 is important for epitaxial diamond growth in part because H radicals present in the plasma will preferentially etch non-diamond graphitic C, allowing only sp3 diamond to grow [44, 45]. In addition, pure H2 plasmas have been used to etch diamond surfaces (e.g. Ivanov et al [46]) and have been shown to reduce the sp2 to sp3

C ratio when etching nitrogen incorporated nanocrystalline diamond [47].

The fact that etch yields are enhanced on amorphous carbon implies that it may be possible, contingent on proper hydrogen ion energy control, to perform this treatment cyclically as a form of atomic layer etching. The initial modification step could use argon ions with energy near or even below the sputtering threshold to amorphize the diamond surface. The subsequent removal step would use low energy hydrogen ions to etch away the damaged layer without removing the underlying diamond. This differs from typical ALE schemes which use noble gas ions to remove chemically modified surface atoms. In practice, this scheme might be effective in removing surface contaminants as well as reducing surface roughness. It would

even allow for precise control over etch per cycle, as adjusting the argon ion energy will alter the amorphous layer thickness and therefore the depth of surface modification.

It should be noted that the mechanism of amorphous carbon removal by energetic H+ ions is related to but probably not identical with that observed during the high pressure, high temperature H2 plasma etching of diamond described above. Bataille et al [45], Ivanov et al [46] and Yurov et al [51] report Arrhenius kinetics with activation energies on the order 1–2 eV/molecule. The etch precursor in this case is thought to be thermal H atoms with no significant ion bombardment component due to the many collisions in the relatively high pressure plasma sheath. A more complete analysis would be needed to investigate the relative mechanisms more deeply, but the minimum H+ ion impact kinetic energy of a few eV (see figure 12) to observe etching from H+ ions seems consistent with a thermal activation energy barrier of about 1–2 eV.

## 4. Conclusions

Classical MD simulations were performed with the goal of deepening our understanding of plasma-assisted diamond etching. This is especially important when processing diamond for quantum sensing devices. This is because the performance of the device is extremely sensitive to atomic-scale defects in the near-surface region of the diamond. Therefore, in order to develop and improve plasmaassisted processing techniques of diamond, a fundamental understanding of the relevant plasma–surface interactions is needed.

Several interatomic force fields for diamond were examined in this work. Results are primarily reported for a secondgeneration REBO potential (referred to as REBO2) and a screened REBO potential (referred to as REBO2-S). Results for other potentials can be found in the supplementary information. The relative accuracy of REBO2 versus REBO2-S is assessed by comparing to literature data from beam experiments. REBO2 gives reasonable agreement with experiments for physical sputtering (etching only by Ar+ ions) and etching by hot (2100 K) H atoms and Ar+ ions. It is also demonstrated that amorphous C is more readily etched relative to diamond C.

A major qualitative difference in the behavior of the two potentials appears when considering etching by energetic H+

ions. While REBO2 and REBO2-S both give good agreement with experimental results at low ion energies (below and near threshold), REBO2 overestimates the etch yield at H+ ion energies above 10 eV. Furthermore, the REBO2 force field predicts that the etch yield will increase roughly linearly with the square root of the ion energy, while the experimental results shows completely different behavior. That is, the etch yield remains relatively constant even when the substrate is exposed to 30 eV H+ ion. It should be noted that this behavior

is atypical for an etch yield as a function of ion energy, and highlights some of the subtle complexities of diamond etch by H+ ions. On the other hand, simulations using REBO2- S show good agreement with the experimental etch yields. The difference in the performance of REBO2 and REBO2- S is attributed to the fact that REBO2-S better reproduces the near-surface amorphous layer created by H+ ion etch, keeping the layer more compact and interconnected relative to REBO2. This explanation is supported by careful analysis of the nearsurface region of the MD simulations.

A novel non-equilibrium plasma-driven processing technique is suggested by our simulation results for smoothing diamond surfaces. Given an initially rough diamond surface, exposure of the surface to Ar+ will amorphize and smooth the near-surface region. Next, the amorphous C can be removed via exposure to relatively low energy H+ ions. Given that it was shown that H more readily etches amorphous C as opposed to diamond C, we expect much of the amorphous layer to be etched away, thereby exposing the underlying diamond surface. However, simulations showed that there was still about 1 ML of amorphous hydrogenated carbon on the surface following the proposed method, possibly requiring an additional liquid etching step.

This study demonstrates the utility of using plasma to modify the near-surface region of diamond. Given the strict constraints on surface contamination and degree of atomicscale defects for quantum-grade diamond, plasma processing techniques show great promise in achieving the level of nearsurface quality needed and perhaps for speeding and/or simplifying processing. The qualitative difference in simulation predictions using REBO2 or REBO2-S highlights the difficultly of developing accurate, robust, and transferable interatomic force fields. The development and adoption of machinelearned interatomic potentials (such as DeepMD [52]) coupled with comparison to well-diagnosed beam experiments is
